pr_title: [API Implementation]: Expose general purpose Crc32 APIs
pr_body:
Proposal implementation of #2036 (closes #2036)

## Proposed API
```cs
namespace System.Numerics
{
    public static class BitOperations
    {
        public static uint Crc32C(uint crc, byte data);
        public static uint Crc32C(uint crc, ushort data);
        public static uint Crc32C(uint crc, uint data);
        public static uint Crc32C(uint crc, ulong data);
    }
}
```

## Current state of implementation
* [x] Ref Assembly
* [x] Documentation
* [x] Implementation
  * [x] Hardware Intrinsics
     * [x] SSE 4.2
     * [x] SSE 4.2 x64 
     * [x] ARM
     * [x] ARM x64 
  * [x] Software Fallback 
* [x] Tests

## Usage of Hardware Intrinsics

```h
uint32_t __crc32b (uint32_t a, uint8_t b); // SSE 4.2
uint32_t __crc32cb (uint32_t a, uint8_t b); // ARM

unsigned int _mm_crc32_u16 (unsigned int crc, unsigned short v); // SSE 4.2
uint32_t __crc32ch (uint32_t a, uint16_t b); // ARM

unsigned int _mm_crc32_u32 (unsigned int crc, unsigned int v); // SSE 4.2
uint32_t __crc32ch (uint32_t a, uint32_t b); // ARM

unsigned __int64 _mm_crc32_u64 (unsigned __int64 crc, unsigned __int64 v); // SSE 4.2 x64
uint32_t __crc32cd (uint32_t a, uint64_t b); // ARM x64
```

## Software Fallback 
```cs
            foreach (byte b in bytes)
            {
                int tableIndex = (int)((crc ^ b) & 0xFF);
                crc = s_crcTable[tableIndex] ^ (crc >> 8);
            }
```

review_comments: I'm not sure right now why this change was made (probably automatically by VS), but it doesn't hurt I think.
Out of curiosity, how did you generate these expected results? What was your "source of truth" for this algorithm?
It was the trust in this algorithm. More simply, I don't think my CPU is lying to me.
Some tests fail here due casting ulong to uint. Is there a Sse42 X64 equivalent for calculating a Crc checksum to uint?

There is no Crc32C support which returns `uint32_t` with data paremter of type `__int64`.
See [Intel® Intrinsics Guide](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/intrinsics-guide/index.html#techs=MMX,SSE,SSE2,SSE3,SSSE3,SSE4_1,SSE4_2,AVX,AVX2,FMA,AVX_VNNI,AVX_512,KNC,AMX,SVML,Other&text=crc)
I removed this.
`_mm_crc32_u64` returns `__int64`, of which only the low 32 bits are populated.  It can be truncated safely.
@saucecontrol Does this return the Castagnoli variant?

Yes, it's the same instruction as emitted by `_mm_crc32_u32`, just with different encoding to indicate it operates on 64 bits instead of 32.  See https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/crc32.

> Starting with an initial value in the first operand (destination operand), accumulates a CRC32 (polynomial 11EDC6F41H) value for the second operand (source operand) and stores the result in the destination operand. The source operand can be a register or a memory location. The destination operand must be an r32 or r64 register. **If the destination is an r64 register, then the 32-bit result is stored in the least significant double word** and 00000000H is stored in the most significant double word of the r64 register.
@saucecontrol I have adjusted this. Does this correspond to your suggestion?

You don't need `Unsafe.As` there.  If you were getting errors on a normal cast from `ulong` to `uint`, you might just need an `unchecked` context, although I don't believe that's necessary in CoreLib.

I think this part could be SIMD-vectorized, if supported on CPU. There are CPUs that support SSE and SSE2 but not SSE4.2. For this case this is relevant in my eyes.

## Example intrinsics

### SSE
```h
__m128 _mm_and_ps (__m128 a, __m128 b);
```

### SSE2
```h
__m128i _mm_and_si128 (__m128i a, __m128i b);
```

### AVX
```h
__m256 _mm256_and_ps (__m256 a, __m256 b);
```

### AVX2
```h
__m256i _mm256_and_si256 (__m256i a, __m256i b);
```
It's a one-time cost, and a small one at that.  Not worth the added complexity even if it could be vectorized.

That it is a one-time cost is true. But vectorizing it would not be a big effort in my opinion, since we have Vector* classes.
